What Scale Is My Miniature?

Another tool I built because I needed it myself

Downloaded an STL with no scale listed, or printed a model that looks wrong next to your army? Measure its height in millimetres — from your slicer's bounding box or a ruler on the printed figure — and this tool tells you which tabletop scale it matches: 28mm, 32mm heroic, 35mm Legion, 40mm Shatterpoint, 1:35 model kits, and everything in between. It compares your measurement against the same 175cm human baseline (eyes at 160cm) that powers every conversion on this site, then hands you a ready-made link to scale it to any game you play. No uploads, no accounts, no cookies.

Direct answer

How to tell what scale a miniature is

Measure from the bottom of the feet to eye level in millimetres. That number is the gaming scale: a model that measures 28mm to the eyes is 28mm scale, 32mm to the eyes is 32mm heroic, 35mm is Legion, 40mm is Shatterpoint. If you only have the total height, subtract about 8-10% for the forehead, helmet, and hair before comparing.

Same 175cm human baseline as the rest of the site — eyes at 160cm. Ratio scales (1:35, 1:56, 1:48…) measure to the top of the head, gaming scales measure to the eyes.

How to measure your model

  1. 1

    If it's still in your slicer — no measuring needed

    Import the STL and read the bounding-box height in millimetres. That's your measurement. STL files carry no units, so this readout is the ground truth for a digital model.

  2. 2

    If it's already printed — use the eye line

    A ruler or caliper from the bottom of the feet to eye level gives the most reliable answer for gaming scales. Measure to the top of the head if that's easier, then pick the "Top of head" option and the tool adjusts for the ~8-10% difference.

  3. 3

    Stuck with an unknown STL? Use the reference bar

    Print the scale reference bar, import it next to your model in Lychee or Chitubox, and read the height off the 5mm ticks. Then come back here to name the scale.

Scale Identification FAQ

How do I find out what scale a miniature is?

Measure from the bottom of the feet to eye level in millimetres — that number is the gaming scale. A 28mm miniature measures 28mm to the eyes, a 32mm heroic model measures 32mm. If you can only measure total height, subtract roughly 8-10% for the forehead, helmet, and hair.

What scale is a 35mm tall miniature?

If 35mm is measured to eye level, it is 35mm scale — used by Star Wars: Legion and Marvel: Crisis Protocol. If 35mm is the total height, it is most likely a 32mm heroic model, because top-of-head runs about 10% above eye level and 32mm models usually stand 34-35mm total.

What scale is a 25mm miniature?

25mm is the classic vintage true scale used by older metal ranges before scale creep pushed the hobby to 28mm. To mix it with a modern 28mm collection, scale it up to about 112% in your slicer.

What scale is a 40mm miniature?

40mm to eye level is the biggest common skirmish scale, used by Star Wars: Shatterpoint and Marvel: Crisis Protocol characters. It is noticeably larger than Warhammer's 32mm heroic.

Why can't I tell the scale from an STL file?

STL files are unitless — they store 3D geometry coordinates but no inches, millimetres, or scale label. Your slicer assumes the units are millimetres, which is why a downloaded file can come out looking like a giant or a grain of rice. Measuring the imported model in the slicer is the only reliable way to identify it.

How do I measure a miniature's scale without digital calipers?

A plain ruler works for most miniatures. Hold it against the model's eye line (not the helmet) and read the millimetres from the base of the feet. For printed models still in the slicer, the bounding-box height readout is even easier — no measuring at all.
